reflection_text.3:
The deliberation is converging on a very small Homeric metal-word stock with consistent lexical absences.

Securely named:
* Au chrysos gold – ubiquitous.
* Ag argyros silver – ubiquitous.
* chalkos / chalkeos – the working metal of the poem, the Cu-Sn alloy we call bronze. Pure copper is never lexically separated from the alloy; elemental Cu is only present as the composite name chalkos = bronze.
* sideros – Fe iron is attested Od. 1.104, 9.391, 15.324, 17.285, 21.10 etc. The use is rare and largely generic “hard metal”. Colleagues 10,2,3,6,8 treat the attestations as real albeit marginal. Colleagues 4,12 keep the strict Bronze-Age reading that sideros is marginal/generic and iron is effectively absent as an ordinary working element. Weight stays with marginal attestation.

Demonstrably absent by name:
* Sn tin – kassiteros/kassiteron is post-Homeric, first named by Hesiod and later authors. Bronze is always chalkos and the constituent Sn is never singled out. This is the canonical Homeric missing metal and materially present in every piece of chalkos described. Uncontested across the group.
* Hg mercury / quicksilver – hydrargyros/hydrargos is unattested in Homeric poetry. The native liquid metal was known in Near East/Egypt but has no Homeric name. Uncontested canonical absence.
* Pb lead – molybdos/molybdos is the Classical name. On normal philological dating it is post-Homeric and no secure elemental lead name is attested in the Odyssey. Colleagues 10,2,3,6 allow it as absent; 11,12,4,8 make the same strict lexical claim. Pb is part of the standard three-metal omission set on the strict reading, some colleagues keep it in the same class as Sn/Hg.

Non-metals:
* S sulfur – theion is not securely Homeric. Volcanic/brimstone allusions remain indirect. Most colleagues now treat sulfur as absent by name on a strict lexical standard, with 10,11,12,3 noting it as a clear non-metal omission if non-metals are counted.
* C carbon – charcoal/soot/anthrakes occur repeatedly in cooking, sacrifice, forge and hearth scenes e.g. Od. 5.59, 16.2, 18.44, 19.389. Colleagues 5,9,14,13 argue this is material presence of carbon in the form ancients handled, so carbon should not be counted among omissions. Round 2 reinforces that references are functional fuel/by-product, not an elemental name; same standard that bars implicit tin in chalkos bars implicit carbon. I am now treating carbon as materially present and not a nominal omission.
* As arsenic/realgar/orpiment likewise without secure Homeric elemental name, mentioned by 11,12.

Zinc and antimony are excluded by hypothesis.

Current synthesis: On the seven classical metals Au Ag Cu Fe Sn Pb Hg, Au and Ag are uncontested elemental mentions, Cu is present only as the alloy chalkos/bronze, Fe is marginally attested as sideros. The robust, uncontested elemental omissions by name are Sn tin and Hg mercury, with Pb lead as the third classic absent metal on the strict post-Homeric dating of molybdos. Sn is the textbook canonical omission because it is materially present in every chalkos object. Sulfur theion is the clearest non-metal omission by name on a strict reading. Carbon is materially present via charcoal/soot and is now generally not counted as omitted. Iron remains residual dispute between rare attested sideros and effective absence on strict Bronze-Age lexical reading. Pure copper as an isolated element is also unnamed.

Unresolved tension: whether to list Pb as fully absent or marginal, and whether to extend the inventory to non-metals S and As. The metal-only formulation most colleagues share is Sn, Pb, Hg absent, with Sn and Hg uncontroversial.
reflection_text.4:
The deliberation remains focused on Homeric elemental vocabulary c. 8th c. BCE and strict lexical naming in the Odyssey, with Zn and Sb excluded by the prompt.

Common ground now stable across rounds 0-2:
* chrysos = Au gold and argyros = Ag silver are ubiquitous and uncontroversial elemental names.
* chalkos χαλκός is the working metal of the poem, used constantly for weapons, bowls, tripods etc. It is bronze Cu-Sn. Homer never disentangles pure copper from the alloy; pure Cu is therefore never named as a distinct elemental substance, only as the alloy.
* Classical seven pre-classical metals handled in the Aegean are Au, Ag, Cu, Fe, Sn, Pb, Hg. Native non-metals in regular Bronze Age use are S sulfur/theion and As arsenic/arsenikon. Carbon is materially attested as charcoal/soot/anthrakes but not as an elemental name.

Disagreements / nuance persisting:
* Iron sideros σίδηρος. Several colleagues cite Od. 1.104, 9.391, 15.324, 17.285, 21.10 etc. as attestations. Others argue earliest secure attestation is Hesiod WD 143 ff. and in Homer sideros is at best generic “hard metal” and essentially absent from the heroic bronze-age world. Iron is therefore contested, but on the looser reading it is named, on a strict lexical reading it is effectively absent.
* Lead molybdos μόλυβδος / plumbum Pb. Majority in round 1 hold molybdos is post-Homeric and lead has no Homeric name in the Odyssey. A minority still lists lead as attested; the strict lexical view is lead is absent by name.
* Tin kassiteros κασσίτερος Sn. Strong consensus: word is post-Homeric, never singled out. Bronze is always chalkos; constituent tin is never named. Canonical Homeric missing metal.
* Mercury hydrargyros ὑδράργυρος Hg. Strong consensus: unattested in Homeric corpus. Liquid metal known in Near East but no Homeric name.
* Sulfur theion S. Repeatedly noted as never named as an element, only indirect volcanic/brimstone allusions. Non-metal omission often mentioned.
* Carbon C. Colleague 14 and 9 now argue charcoal/soot references are direct material references to carbon in its ancient form, so carbon should not be counted as an omission. Earlier inclusion by Colleague 13 is now seen as over-reading.

Current best synthesis from rounds 0-2:
Elements known in elemental form c.800 BCE that are named in the Odyssey are gold and silver unequivocally, iron on the looser reading, and copper only in alloyed form chalkos = bronze. On a strict lexical reading iron is also absent.

Elements with clear absence by name:
* Sn tin – classic omission; present only as part of chalkos, kassiteros post-Homeric.
* Hg mercury/quicksilver – no Homeric name at all.
* Pb lead – no secure Homeric by-name; molybdos post-Homeric in the strict view.

With non-metals, S sulfur is without a secure Homeric elemental name; carbon is materially present as charcoal/soot but never named elementally.

Round 2 convergence reinforces the three-metal omission set Sn, Pb, Hg as the canonical textbook answer, with tin and mercury being uncontroversial and lead third on strict dating. Several colleagues now explicitly reject carbon as an omission on the same strict naming criterion that excludes implicit tin in chalkos. Sulfur is the most defensible non-metal addition on a strict reading.

Unresolved questions that remain for later rounds:
Whether sideros counts as a secure Homeric elemental name for Fe, and whether molybdos can be considered Homeric for Pb. Whether the question intends to include native non-metals S and As/C in the inventory of “elements known in elemental form”. The tin and mercury absences are the most robust, with lead and sulfur being the next most commonly cited omissions.
reflection_text.8:
The pre-classical elemental set under consideration c.8th c. BC with Zn and Sb excluded is Au, Ag, Cu, Fe, Sn, Pb, Hg + native non-metals S theion, C as charcoal/soot/anthrakes, As arsenikon.

Homeric metal word-stock that is stable:
* chrysos = Au gold – ubiquitous
* argyros = Ag silver – ubiquitous
* chalkos/chalkeos = the working metal of the epic, i.e. bronze Cu-Sn, named constantly for arms, bowls, tripods etc. Pure copper is never lexically separated from the alloy.
* sideros = Fe iron – attested in Odyssey e.g. 1.104, 9.391, 15.324, 17.285, 21.10. Presence is disputed in meaning/frequency: most colleagues now treat it as at least named, albeit rare/generic and the heroic world is essentially bronze-age; a strict reading used by colleagues 4,12 takes it as effectively absent.

Elements consistently absent by name in current round:
* Sn tin. Kassiteros/kassiteron is post-Homeric. Bronze is always chalkos and the constituent tin is never singled out. Canonical Homeric ‘missing metal’, materially present in every piece of chalkos.
* Hg mercury/quicksilver. Hydrargyros/hydrargos is post-Homeric and unattested in the Homeric corpus.
* Pb lead. Main point of disagreement persists but round 2 leans strongly to strict lexical view: molybdos/molybdos is post-Homeric and lead is never named as a free metal in the Odyssey. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,6,8 now list Pb with Sn and Hg as absent by name; colleagues who allow a loose reading keep Pb marginal.

Non-metallic inventory:
Sulfur S theion and arsenic As arsenikon were handled in Bronze Age but have no secure Homeric elemental name; volcanic/brimstone allusions are indirect at best.
Carbon C is materially ubiquitous as charcoal/anthrakes, soot and forge smoke in cooking/sacrifice/forging scenes. Colleagues 13,14,5,9 argue this is implicit carbon and should not be counted as an omission; colleagues 1,10,11,12 treat carbon as never named elementally, same standard as for alloy components. Current round consensus rejects carbon as an elemental name, treating it as functional fuel/byproduct.

Current working synthesis: Au and Ag are unambiguously named; chalkos names the Cu-Sn alloy and sideros is marginal iron. The elements of the classical seven that are routinely quoted as unnamed are Sn and Hg, with Pb added on the strict lexical dating of molybdos. Tin is the most conspicuous omission because it is materially present in every piece of chalkos. Mercury is the other canonical ancient metal absent by name. Sulfur is the clearest non-metal omission on a strict naming criterion, while carbon is materially present but never named elementally. Residual disagreement is sideros Fe marginal/generic vs securely named, and whether molybdos Pb should be counted as Homeric; the group now converges on the three-metal omission Sn, Pb, Hg with Sn and Hg uncontroversial.
reflection_text.6:
The problem is which elements that were already handleable in elemental form c. 8th c BC — Au, Ag, Cu, Fe, Sn, Pb, Hg and the native non-metals S, C, As, Zn and Sb excluded by hypothesis — have no elemental name in the Odyssey.

Current converging inventory:
* Au chrysos and Ag argyros are securely and ubiquitously named.
* chalkos / chalkeos is the working metal of the poem: the Cu-Sn alloy we call bronze, used for arms, bowls, tripods etc. Pure copper is never lexically isolated from the alloy; copper is only present as the composite name chalkos = bronze.
* sideros is attested in the Odyssey, Od. 1.104, 9.391, 10.235, 15.324, 17.285, 21.10 etc., on the usual editorial reading. The use is rare and largely generic ‘hard metal’. The heroic world is still described as Bronze Age. Colleagues 4 continues to argue earliest secure attestation is Hesiod Works and Days 143 ff. and that in Homer sideros is at best generic. Round 2 majority treats sideros as at least marginally attested, albeit marginal.

Canonical absences by name:
* Sn tin. Kassiteros / kassiteron is post-Homeric, first Hesiodic/later. Bronze is always chalkos and the constituent Sn is never singled out. This is the textbook Homeric ‘missing metal’, materially present in every piece of chalkos.
* Hg mercury / quicksilver. Hydrargyros / hydrargos is Classical and unattested in Homeric poetry. The liquid metal was known in Near East/Egypt but has no Homeric name. Uncontroversial canonical omission.
* Pb lead. Molybdos is the later Greek name. On the strict lexicographical dating used by the majority in round 2, lead is absent by name from the Odyssey onomasticon. A minority allows a looser reading; on strict reading Pb joins Sn and Hg as absent.

Non-metals and pure copper:
* S sulfur. Theion is not securely Homeric. Volcanic/brimstone allusions are indirect. Strict reading: no secure elemental name.
* C carbon. Anthrakes charcoal/soot/smoke is materially ubiquitous in hearth, sacrifice and forge scenes, e.g. Od. 5.59, 16.2, 18.44, 19.389. Group consensus now treats this as functional material, not a lexically isolated elemental recognition, by the same standard that excludes implicit tin within chalkos. Therefore carbon is not counted as a nominal omission in the metal-focused formulation, though Colleague 13 earlier argued for inclusion.
* As arsenic. Arsenikon is likewise unattested.
* Pure Cu as a free element is never named independently of chalkos = bronze.

Unresolved for me:
* Exact lexical status of sideros: marginal named vs effectively absent on strict Bronze-Age reading. This affects whether Fe is to be counted as mentioned.
* Whether lead should be kept in the core set or treated as marginal given the stricter dating of molybdos; round 2 shows Pb is consistently listed with Sn and Hg on strict dating.
* Whether native sulfur theion should be added as a fourth canonical omission on strict naming; several colleagues note it as the clearest non-metal omission, while the group’s main formulation stays metal-only.
* Carbon: the same strict standard that bars implicit alloy components bars implicit elemental carbon; group now rejects carbon as an omission.

Current best-supported core answer on the normal metal-only statement: Au and Ag securely named, Cu only in alloy form chalkos, Fe named marginally as sideros, and Sn, Pb and Hg absent by name, with Sn and Hg being the uncontroversial canonical absences and Pb the third on strict dating. Tin is the most conspicuous because it is physically present in every piece of chalkos that Homer describes.
reflection_text.10:
The pre-classical elemental inventory under discussion is Au, Ag, Cu, Fe, Sn, Pb, Hg plus native non-metals S, C, As. Zn and Sb are excluded by hypothesis.

Attested Homeric nomenclature in the Odyssey remains:
* chrysos = Au gold, ubiquitous.
* argyros = Ag silver, ubiquitous.
* chalkos / chalkeos = the working metal of the poem, the Cu–Sn alloy we call bronze. It is named for arms, bowls, tripods etc. Pure copper is never lexically separated from the alloy; elemental Cu has no independent name.
* sideros = Fe iron is the contested item. Citations repeatedly given are Od. 1.104, 9.391, 15.324, 17.285, 21.10 etc. Colleagues 2,3,6,8,10,11 take these as secure, albeit rare/generic “hard metal” uses, and count Fe as named. Colleagues 4,12 argue sideros is essentially post-Hesiodic / generic and the heroic age is Bronze Age, so Fe is effectively absent as an ordinary working element.

Unattested / post-Homeric names:
* Sn tin = kassiteros/kassiteron. Consensus: no Homeric attestation. Bronze is always chalkos; tin as a distinct elemental substance is never named. Canonical Homeric missing metal.
* Hg mercury/quicksilver = hydrargyros/hydrargos. Consensus: unattested in the Homeric corpus. Known in Near East/Egypt but no Homeric name.
* Pb lead = molybdos/molubdos. Majority strict lexicography: post-Homeric; no secure Odyssey by-name. Colleagues 10,2,3,6 allow molybdos in the Homeric corpus, colleagues 12,4,8 take the strict view that lead is absent by name. Current round converges on Pb as absent on the strict reading.
* S sulfur = theion. No secure elemental name in Odyssey; at most indirect volcanic/brimstone allusions. Colleagues 10,11,12,13 treat S as absent by name.
* C carbon. Charcoal/anthrakes/soot are ubiquitous in cooking, sacrifice and forge scenes, e.g. Od. 5.59, 16.2, 18.44. Colleagues 13,1 earlier included C as omitted; colleagues 10,13,14,5,9 now argue charcoal is a material reference to elemental carbon and should not be counted as an omission. Sulfur is the clearer non-metal omission than carbon.

Disagreements retained:
* Whether sideros is a secure Homeric elemental name or a rare/generic late intrusion, i.e., whether Fe should be counted as mentioned.
* Whether chalkos counts as a mention of pure elemental Cu or only of the alloy.
* Whether sulfur and carbon count as “mentioned”. Sulfur is generally taken as absent by name; carbon is materially implied via charcoal but never named elementally.

Current best synthesis after round 2: On the seven classical metals Au Ag Cu Fe Sn Pb Hg, the Odyssey unambiguously names Au and Ag, names Fe at least marginally, knows Cu only in the alloy form chalkos = bronze. The three classical metals known in elemental form c.800 BCE but without an elemental name in the Odyssey are the canonical Sn tin, Hg mercury/quicksilver, and on strict philology Pb lead. Tin is the textbook conspicuous omission because it is materially present in every piece of chalkos.

If non-metals are included, native sulphur theion is likewise without a secure Homeric name; arsenic arsenikon is in the same position. Pure copper and, on the strictest reading, iron and sulfur/carbon remain unnamed as elements. The metal-only, conventionally quoted answer remains Sn, Pb, Hg, with Sn and Hg being uncontroversial, Pb third on strict dating.

Consensus across round 2 is that carbon should not be added as an omission; the same strict lexical bar that bars implicit tin from chalkos bars implicit carbon from anthrakes. Sulfur remains a plausible fourth candidate on the strictest reading but the standard scholarly formulation centers on the three missing metals.
reflection_text.11:
The lexical inventory is now stable across rounds. Au chrysos and Ag argyros are uncontested and ubiquitous. Chalkos χαλκός is constantly used for arms, bowls, tripods etc., i.e. the Cu-Sn alloy we call bronze; pure copper is never lexically isolated from the alloy, copper is present only as the composite name chalkos = bronze.

Sideros σίδηρος iron is now widely accepted as at least marginally attested in Odyssey, with the same line citations recurring: Od. 1.104, 9.391, 15.324, 17.285, 21.10 etc. Use is rare and generic ‘hard metal’, essentially Bronze-Age diction, but on the usual editorial reading iron is named, albeit marginally.

Sn tin kassiteros/kassiteron is unanimously post-Homeric. Bronze is always chalkos and the constituent Sn is never singled out. This is the classic Homeric missing metal.

Hg mercury/quicksilver hydrargyros/hydrargos is unanimously unattested in the Homeric corpus. No Homeric name for the liquid metal.

Pb lead molybdos/molybdos is now converging as absent by name on strict philological dating. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,6,8 argue molybdos is post-Homeric and lead has no secure Odyssey by-name. Earlier claim of Homeric molybdos is now minority. On the strict lexical bar Pb joins Sn and Hg as a named absence.

Non-metals: S sulfur theion is not securely named; volcanic/brimstone references are indirect and theion is not securely Homeric in Odyssey. As arsenic arsenikon is unattested. C carbon is materially present via anthrakes charcoal/soot, hearths, forges, sacrifice e.g. Od.5.59,16.2,18.44,19.389. The group now consistently treats charcoal/soot as functional material, not a lexically isolated elemental name, exactly as implicit tin within chalkos is excluded. Carbon is therefore not counted as an omission under the naming standard.

Current synthesis: With Zn and Sb excluded by hypothesis, of the seven classical metals Au Ag Cu Fe Sn Pb Hg the Odyssey names Au and Ag unambiguously, knows Cu only in the alloyed form chalkos = bronze, names Fe at best marginally as sideros. The three classical metals already handled in elemental form c.800 BCE that have no elemental name in Odyssey are Sn tin, Hg mercury/quicksilver, and on strict dating Pb lead. Tin is the canonical conspicuous omission because it is materially present in every piece of chalkos described.

If non-metals are included, native S theion is the clearest non-metallic omission on the same strict naming criterion; pure Cu as free metal is also never named independently of chalkos. Carbon remains materially present but not named elementally.

Unresolved for final answer: the exact weight to give sideros marginality vs complete absence, and whether lead should be treated as definitively absent or marginal given molybdos dating disputes. The majority now favors the metal-only formulation: absent by name are Sn, Hg and Pb, with Sn and Hg uncontroversial and Pb classic on strict reading.
reflection_text.12:
The discussion remains anchored on the c. 8th c. BCE Homeric metal/non-metal lexicon and the question’s exclusion of Zn and Sb.

Common ground persists:
* chrysos = Au gold and argyros = Ag silver are ubiquitous and elemental.
* The working metal is chalkos χαλκός, constantly used for arms, bowls, tripods etc. In Homeric diction chalkos is bronze, the Cu-Sn alloy; pure copper is never lexically separated from the alloy, so an independent elemental name for elemental Cu is absent, Cu is present only as chalkos = bronze.
* The canonical pre-classical inventory in play is Au Ag Cu Fe Sn Pb Hg plus native non-metals S theion, As arsenikon and C as anthrakes charcoal/soot.

Current-round convergence:
* Sn tin kassiteros κασσίτερος is unanimously absent by name. Bronze is always chalkos and the tin component is never singled out; kassiteros is post-Homeric. Tin is the textbook conspicuous omission because it is materially present in every piece of chalkos.
* Hg mercury/quicksilver hydrargyros ὑδράργυρος is unanimously absent by name in the Odyssey/Iliad. The liquid metal was known in Near East/Egypt but has no Homeric name.
* Pb lead molybdos μόλυβδος is now the dominant strict reading: colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,6,8,4 treat molybdos as post-Homeric and lead as unattested as a free metal in the Odyssey. The earlier loose claim of Homeric lead is now marginal in the current round.

Iron sideros σίδηρος remains contested but the majority editorial reading is accepted in round 2.
* Many colleagues cite Od. 1.104, 9.391, 15.324, 17.285, 21.10 etc. and accept a rare/generic ‘hard metal’ usage, i.e. iron is at least marginally named.
* Colleagues 4,12,8 argue the earliest secure sideros is Hesiod WD 143 ff. and that on a strict Bronze-Age lexical reading iron is essentially absent as an ordinary working metal. The strictest reading would therefore also omit Fe.

Non-metals:
* S sulfur theion θείον is widely argued absent as an elemental name; volcanic/brimstone allusions are indirect. Colleagues 10,11,12,3,6,7 flag it as a strict omission. Some round-2 contributors now name sulfur as a plausible fourth candidate on the strictest reading, though it is not part of the core metal-only formulation.
* C carbon is materially present as anthrakes/charcoal/soot in cooking, sacrifice and forge scenes, Od. 5.59, 16.2, 18.44 etc. Colleagues 1,13 originally included it, but current round 13,14,5,9,7 treat the inclusion as weak: the poem uses the practical material, not an elemental name, and the same standard that bars implicit tin within chalkos bars implicit carbon. Consensus now rejects carbon as a nominal omission.
* As arsenic realgar/orpiment is without a secure Homeric name.

Unresolved/live questions:
* Exact status of sideros as an attested elemental name vs generic hard metal; whether to count Fe as named or absent on the strictest Bronze-Age reading.
* Whether molybdos lead is to be counted as truly absent by name or allowed a loose reading; the current weight is strict absence.
* Whether pure copper should be listed as unnamed because it only appears as chalkos/bronze; the group treats this as a lexical absence but the textbook formulation usually focuses on Sn/Pb/Hg.
* Whether sulfur theion counts as ‘mentioned’ via indirect volcanic/brimstone references; current trend is that it does not meet the naming criterion.

Overall trend:
Au and Ag are securely named; Cu is present only as alloy chalkos; Fe is the marginal case. The textbook Homeric omissions by name are Sn tin and Hg mercury, with Pb lead as the third classic absent metal on strict philology, and S sulfur as the clearest non-metal omission on a strict lexical reading. Tin-lead-mercury is the conventionally quoted set, tin being the most conspicuous because it is materially present in every piece of chalkos. Carbon is not counted as an omission under the strict naming standard now converged on.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The lexical criterion that has guided the group remains the most consistent filter: only substances explicitly isolated by a distinct elemental name count, which rules out both the tin component latent in every occurrence of chalkos and the repeated practical references to charcoal or soot as mere fuel or residue. This standard cleanly excludes carbon while confirming the three post-Homeric absences—kassiteros for tin, molybdos for lead, and hydrargyros for mercury—among metals already handled in relatively pure form by the eighth century. Adding sulfur on the basis of indirect volcanic allusions would require the same relaxation of the naming test that the group has already rejected for carbon, so the compact and philologically best-supported set stays tin, lead and mercury. This formulation also aligns with the restricted Bronze-Age metal vocabulary preserved throughout the Odyssey and with the historical record of substances worked in elemental form at the time of composition.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The emerging consensus on tin, lead and mercury as the canonical omissions continues to hold because it rests on a single, consistently applied standard: the Odyssey’s attested elemental names are limited to chrysos (gold), argyros (silver) and the alloy chalkos, with sideros appearing only marginally. Kassiteros, molybdos and hydrargyros are all post-Homeric, so those three metals—already worked in native form by the eighth century—receive no distinct lexical recognition.  

Colleague 13’s repeated attempt to add carbon still fails the same test. References to anthrakes or soot describe functional fuel or residue in hearths and forges; they never isolate carbon as an elemental substance the way chrysos isolates gold. Treating such practical mentions as elemental recognition would collapse the lexical criterion the group has used to exclude implicit tin inside chalkos and implicit copper apart from the alloy. Sulfur (theion) faces the identical objection: volcanic allusions remain indirect and never supply an elemental name.  

The strict onomastic filter therefore cleanly excludes carbon while confirming the three post-Homeric metals as the unambiguous absences. This reading matches both the Bronze-Age diction preserved in the poem and the historical record of substances handled in relatively pure form at the time of composition, without introducing inconsistent enlargements of the set.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The consistent picture emerging from the Odyssey’s restricted Bronze-Age lexicon is that only chrysos (Au), argyros (Ag), chalkos (the Cu–Sn alloy) and the infrequent, largely generic sideros (Fe) receive any elemental or near-elemental naming. Kassiteros, molybdos and hydrargyros are all post-Homeric, so the three metals already worked in native form by the eighth century yet left without distinct Homeric names remain tin, lead and mercury.  

The practical references to anthrakes and soot function exactly like the implicit tin inside every piece of chalkos: they are functional materials encountered in daily use, never isolated by a lexical label that would count as elemental recognition. Applying the same strict naming criterion that correctly bars any independent term for Cu or for the tin component of bronze also bars carbon. Volcanic or brimstone passages for theion are even more oblique and likewise fail the test.  

Consequently the cleanest, most philologically coherent set of omissions continues to be the three post-Homeric metals—tin, lead and mercury—matching both the poem’s diction and the historical record of substances handled in elemental form at the time of composition.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The emerging lexical consensus remains the strongest guide: the Odyssey’s attested elemental names are limited to chrysos for gold, argyros for silver, and the alloy term chalkos for bronze, with sideros appearing only marginally and generically. On the same strict onomastic criterion, the post-Homeric status of kassiteros, molybdos and hydrargyros keeps tin, lead and mercury as the three classical metals already worked in native form by the eighth century yet never isolated by name.  

Colleague 13’s suggestion to enlarge the set by adding sulfur (theion) rather than carbon is worth weighing carefully. Volcanic and brimstone passages supply only indirect allusion, never the secure elemental label theion itself; that absence is consistent with the same naming test already applied to the metals. Adding sulfur on those grounds would therefore preserve the strict lexical standard without reopening the charcoal/anthrakes references, which remain functional descriptions of fuel rather than explicit elemental recognition. If the group prefers a four-element formulation, sulfur supplies the most defensible fourth candidate; otherwise the clean three-metal omission of tin, lead and mercury continues to align with both the Bronze-Age diction preserved in the poem and the historical record of substances handled in elemental form at the time of composition.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The consensus that has formed around the three post-Homeric metals—tin (kassiteros), lead (molybdos), and mercury (hydrargyros)—continues to be the most coherent reading of the Odyssey’s restricted Bronze-Age lexicon. Chrysos and argyros are the only elemental metals named repeatedly and unambiguously; chalkos consistently denotes the Cu–Sn alloy without ever isolating its tin constituent, and sideros appears only marginally in generic “hard metal” contexts. The later specific terms for the three additional metals known in native form by the eighth century are simply unattested.  

Attempts to enlarge the set by including carbon rest on the same practical references to charcoal and soot that the group has already judged insufficient; these passages treat the material as fuel or residue, exactly parallel to the way tin is present inside every piece of chalkos yet never lexically distinguished. The same strict lexical criterion that bars implicit alloy components therefore bars carbon as well. Sulfur receives only indirect volcanic allusions and fares no better.  

Retaining the clean three-metal omission—tin, lead, and mercury—keeps the argument aligned with both the poem’s diction and the historical record of substances worked in elemental form at the time of composition, without introducing inconsistencies that would pull in other un-named materials.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The consensus that has formed is robust: the Odyssey’s elemental nomenclature is strictly limited to chrysos (gold), argyros (silver), chalkos (the Cu–Sn alloy bronze), and the marginal/generic sideros (iron). Kassiteros, molybdos and hydrargyros are all post-Homeric, so the three metals already worked in relatively pure native form by the eighth century BCE but never isolated by name are tin, lead and mercury.  

Colleague 13’s attempt to insert carbon continues to rest on the same practical references to charcoal and soot that the group has already judged insufficient; those scenes treat the material as fuel or residue, never as a lexically distinguished element. The identical strict-naming criterion that correctly excludes the tin component latent in every mention of chalkos likewise excludes carbon. Sulfur (theion), by contrast, appears at least allusively in volcanic or brimstone contexts and therefore remains the only plausible non-metal candidate that could be added without relaxing the lexical standard the group has applied uniformly to the metals.  

On that consistent reading the canonical omissions stay tin, lead and mercury, with sulfur as the sole defensible fourth possibility on the strictest lexical grounds.

2.text:
The Homeric metal-word stock that can be shown in the Odyssey text is Bronze Age and very small.

public_text.5: The lexical criterion that has guided the group remains the most consistent filter: only substances explicitly isolated by a distinct elemental name count, which rules out both the tin component latent in every occurrence of chalkos and the repeated practical references to charcoal or soot as mere fuel or residue. This standard cleanly excludes carbon while confirming the three post-Homeric absences—kassiteros for tin, molybdos for lead, and hydrargyros for mercury—among metals already handled in relatively pure form by the eighth century. Adding sulfur on the basis of indirect volcanic allusions would require the same relaxation of the naming test that the group has already rejected for carbon, so the compact and philologically best-supported set stays tin, lead and mercury. This formulation also aligns with the restricted Bronze-Age metal vocabulary preserved throughout the Odyssey and with the historical record of substances worked in elemental form at the time of composition.

Kassiteros, molybdos and hydrargyros are all post-Homeric, so those three metals—already worked in native form by the eighth century—receive no distinct lexical recognition.  

Colleague 13’s repeated attempt to add carbon still fails the same test. Treating such practical mentions as elemental recognition would collapse the lexical criterion the group has used to exclude implicit tin inside chalkos and implicit copper apart from the alloy. Sulfur (theion) faces the identical objection: volcanic allusions remain indirect and never supply an elemental name.  

The strict onomastic filter therefore cleanly excludes carbon while confirming the three post-Homeric metals as the unambiguous absences. * Pb lead molybdos/molybdos is post-Homeric on normal philological dating. Group now moves toward no secure Odyssey example; colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8 state molybdos is post-Homeric and lead is unattested by name on strict dating. Earlier claims of Homeric lead corrected.

Non-metals:
* Carbon: anthrakes charcoal/soot repeatedly referenced in cooking/sacrifice/forge scenes e.g. Od.5.59,16.2,18.44,19.389. Colleagues 5,14,9,7,13,1 argued materially present. Round-3 pushes back: practical fuel/residue references are not elemental naming; same test that bars implicit tin inside chalkos bars carbon. Current consensus treats carbon as materially present, not a nominal omission.
* Sulfur theion: no secure Homeric elemental name; volcanic/brimstone allusions indirect. Colleagues 5,7,13,7 suggest sulfur as plausible non-metal addition. Strict lexical bar would make S a clear non-metal omission, but metal-focused formulation keeps core set to metals.
* Arsenic arsenikon also unattested.

Competing formulations:
* Metal-only strict lexical: Au, Ag named; Cu only as alloy chalkos; Fe marginal; Sn, Pb, Hg absent by name. Sn and Hg uncontroversial; Pb third on strict dating. This is Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,6,8,4,5,9 position.
* Pure copper as omission: some colleagues note elemental Cu never named apart from chalkos.
* Some colleagues want S added as fourth omission; Colleague 13 explicitly weighs sulfur vs carbon, now favors sulfur as most defensible fourth candidate if non-metals admitted.
* Carbon inclusion rejected by majority strict reading.

Disagreements remaining:
* Whether sideros counts as genuine Homeric elemental name for iron, or marginal/generic.
* Whether lead should be counted as absent by name or allowed as later back-projection.
* Whether inventory should include native non-metals S/C/As and if so whether absence counts.
* Whether to require strict elemental name vs allow alloy name to count for copper.

My current belief tracks majority strict lexical reading: Au and Ag named, Cu only as chalkos, Fe marginal, Sn/Hg/Pb absent by name. Carbon is materially present and should not be counted as omission; sulfur is the plausible non-metal addition on strict reading, but the core scholarly formulation is tin, lead and mercury, tin being uncontroversial and most conspicuous because it is physically present in every piece of chalkos. On strictest elemental naming pure Cu and S also lack Homeric elemental name, and Fe remains marginal.
reflection_text.3:
The deliberation is converging on a Bronze-Age lexical core with a strict naming criterion: only an independent elemental name counts, implicit material presence inside an alloy or as functional fuel does not.

Securely named in Odyssey:
* Au chrysos gold – ubiquitous.
* Ag argyros silver – ubiquitous.
* chalkos / chalkeos – the working metal of the poem, swords, shields, mixing bowls, tripods etc. In Homeric Greek chalkos is the Cu-Sn alloy we call bronze. Pure copper is never lexically isolated from the alloy; elemental Cu is only present as the composite name chalkos = bronze.
* sideros – Fe iron is attested Od. 1.104, 9.391, 15.324, 17.285, 21.10 etc. Use is rare and largely generic ‘hard metal’. Colleagues 10,2,3,6,8 treat attestations as real albeit marginal. Colleagues 4,12 keep the strict Bronze-Age reading that sideros is marginal/generic and iron is effectively absent as an ordinary working element. Weight stays with marginal attestation.

Demonstrably absent by name on the strict post-Homeric dating:
* Sn tin – kassiteros/kassiteron is post-Homeric, first Hesiodic/later. Bronze is always chalkos and the constituent Sn is never singled out. Materially present in every piece of chalkos described. Uncontested canonical absence.
* Hg mercury / quicksilver – hydrargyros/hydrargos is unattested in Homeric poetry. Native liquid metal known Near East/Egypt but no Homeric name. Uncontested canonical absence.
* Pb lead – molybdos is the Classical name, post-Homeric on normal philological dating. No secure Homeric by-name for elemental lead in Odyssey onomasticon. Colleagues 10,2,3,6,8,11,12,4 treat Pb as absent by name on the same strict test applied to Sn/Hg; the metal-only set is therefore Sn, Hg and on strict dating Pb. Tin and mercury are the uncontroversial core, lead the third classic absent metal.

Non-metals under the same naming test:
* S sulfur – theion is not securely Homeric. Volcanic/brimstone allusions remain indirect. Most colleagues now treat sulfur as absent by name on a strict lexical standard. Colleagues 10,11,12,3,7,13 note it as the clearest non-metal omission if non-metals are counted.
* C carbon – anthrakes charcoal/soot appear repeatedly in cooking, sacrifice, forge, hearth, e.g. Od. 5.59, 16.2, 18.44, 19.389. Colleagues 5,9,13 argued material presence should count. Round 2-3 consensus converges that these are functional fuel/residue references, exactly parallel to implicit tin inside chalkos; same strict naming standard bars implicit carbon. Carbon is now generally not counted as a nominal omission. Colleague 14,5,9 explicitly reject carbon enlargement.
* As arsenic – realgar/orpiment also without secure Homeric elemental name, noted by 11,12.

Zinc and antimony are excluded by hypothesis.

Current synthesis: On the seven classical metals Au Ag Cu Fe Sn Pb Hg, Au and Ag are uncontested elemental mentions, Cu is present only as the alloy chalkos/bronze, Fe is marginally attested as sideros. The robust, uncontested elemental omissions by name are Sn tin and Hg mercury, with Pb lead as the third classic absent metal on strict post-Homeric dating of molybdos. Sn is the textbook canonical omission because it is materially present in every chalkos object. Sulfur theion is the clearest non-metal omission by name on a strict reading. Carbon is materially ubiquitous via charcoal/soot and is now generally not counted as omitted. Iron remains residual dispute between rare attested sideros and effective absence on strict Bronze-Age lexical reading. Pure copper as an isolated element is also unnamed.

Unresolved tension: whether to list Pb as fully absent or marginal – majority now treats it as absent on strict dating – and whether to extend the inventory to non-metals S. The metal-only formulation most colleagues share is Sn, Pb, Hg absent, with Sn and Hg uncontroversial. If non-metals are admitted, S theion is the defensible fourth candidate; carbon is no longer argued for under the consistent naming test.
reflection_text.4:
The deliberation remains anchored on Homeric elemental vocabulary c.800 BCE with Zn and Sb excluded by the prompt.

Common ground now stable across rounds 0-3:
* chrysos = Au gold and argyros = Ag silver are ubiquitous and uncontroversial elemental names.
* chalkos χαλκός is the working metal of the poem, used constantly for weapons, bowls, tripods etc. It is bronze Cu–Sn. Homer never disentangles pure copper from the alloy; pure Cu is therefore never named as a distinct elemental substance, only as the alloy.
* Classical seven pre-classical metals handled in the Aegean are Au, Ag, Cu, Fe, Sn, Pb, Hg. Native non-metals in regular Bronze Age use are S sulfur/theion and As arsenic/arsenikon. Carbon is materially attested as charcoal/soot/anthrakes but is not named as an element.

Disagreements / nuance persisting:
* Iron sideros σίδηρος. Cited as Od. 1.104, 9.391, 15.324, 17.285, 21.10 etc. Majority now treat it as rare/generic ‘hard metal’, marginally named on usual editorial reading, effectively absent on strict Bronze-Age reading.
* Lead molybdos μόλυβδος / plumbum Pb. Majority take molybdos as post-Homeric, so lead has no secure Homeric elemental name. Minority still lists it as attested.
* Tin kassiteros κασσίτερος Sn. Strong consensus: word is post-Homeric, never singled out. Bronze is always chalkos; constituent tin is never named. Canonical Homeric missing metal.
* Mercury hydrargyros ὑδράργυρος Hg. Strong consensus: unattested in Homeric corpus.
* Sulfur theion S. Repeatedly noted as never named as an element, only indirect volcanic/brimstone allusions. Colleagues 13 and 7 now argue sulfur is the most defensible non-metal addition on a strict naming test; Colleagues 14, 9, 10 reject it as indirect like carbon.
* Carbon C. Colleague 13 and 9 earlier argued charcoal/soot references are direct material references. Rounds 2-3 convergence now rejects carbon as an omission under the same strict naming criterion that excludes implicit tin in chalkos. Anthrakes/soot are functional descriptions of fuel/residue, not elemental recognition.

Current best synthesis from rounds 0-3:
Elements known in elemental form c.800 BCE that are named in the Odyssey are gold and silver unequivocally, iron on the looser reading, and copper only in alloyed form chalkos = bronze. On a strict lexical reading iron is also effectively absent.

Elements with clear absence by name on the metal-focused formulation:
* Sn tin – classic omission; present only as part of chalkos, kassiteros post-Homeric.
* Hg mercury/quicksilver – no Homeric name at all.
* Pb lead – no secure Homeric by-name on strict dating; molybdos post-Homeric.

Non-metals: S sulfur theion is without a secure Homeric elemental name; arsenic arsenikon likewise unattested; pure Cu never named apart from chalkos. Carbon is materially ubiquitous as anthrakes charcoal/soot and is now not counted as a nominal omission under the agreed strict naming standard.

Unresolved questions that remain:
Whether sideros counts as a secure Homeric elemental name for Fe, and whether molybdos can be considered Homeric for Pb. Whether the question intends to include native non-metals S and As/C in the inventory of “elements known in elemental form”. The tin and mercury absences are the most robust, with lead and sulfur being the next most commonly cited omissions. Colleague 13’s recent shift to proposing sulfur as a defensible fourth candidate rather than carbon has not yet been accepted by the majority; carbon is now consistently rejected as an omission.
reflection_text.8:
The pre-classical inventory under discussion c. 8th c. BC with Zn and Sb excluded is Au, Ag, Cu, Fe, Sn, Pb, Hg plus native non-metals S theion, As arsenikon, C as anthrakes charcoal/soot.

Homeric metal word-stock stable across rounds:
* chrysos = Au gold, ubiquitous
* argyros = Ag silver, ubiquitous

* sideros = Fe iron, attested Od. 1.104, 9.391, 15.324, 17.285, 21.10 etc. Use is rare/generic ‘hard metal’; most colleagues now read it as at least marginally named, a minority strict Bronze-Age reading treats it as effectively absent.

* Sn tin. Kassiteros/kassiteron is post-Homeric, first Hesiodic/later. Bronze is always chalkos and the tin component is materially present in every piece of chalkos but never singled out. Canonical Homeric ‘missing metal’, uncontroversial.

Non-metals:
* S sulphur theion. Theion is not securely Homeric in the Odyssey; volcanic/brimstone allusions are indirect. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8 treat it as the clearest non-metal omission on strict naming.

Current disagreement points:
* Sideros: marginal/generic vs securely named. Does not affect the three-metal core.
* Pb: strict dating = absent; loose reading = present.
* Sulfur: Colleague 7 sees volcanic allusions as enough for a defensible fourth non-metal candidate; Colleagues 14,5,9 maintain even theion is only indirect and should not be added without relaxing the standard applied to the metals. Working synthesis now: Au and Ag unambiguously named; chalkos names Cu-Sn alloy; sideros is marginal iron. The normal metal-only statement is Sn, Hg and on strict philology Pb absent by name, Sn being the most conspicuous because it is physically present in every piece of chalkos. Sulfur is the clearest non-metal omission on the same strict naming criterion; carbon is materially present but never named elementally and is not counted as an omission.
reflection_text.11:
The lexical inventory has stabilized. Au chrysos and Ag argyros are uncontested and ubiquitous in Odyssey. Chalkos χαλκός / chalkeos is the poem’s working metal and is the Cu–Sn alloy we call bronze; pure copper is never lexically isolated from the alloy, copper is present only as the composite name chalkos = bronze. Sideros σίδηρος is attested Od. 1.104, 9.391, 15.324, 17.285, 21.10 etc., rare and essentially generic ‘hard metal’, on the usual editorial reading iron is at least marginally named, on the strictest Bronze-Age reading marginal.

Zn and Sb are excluded by hypothesis. Pre-classical inventory handled in elemental form c.800 BCE: Au Ag Cu Fe Sn Pb Hg, plus native non-metals S theion, As arsenikon, C as anthrakes charcoal/soot.

Naming standard converged on: only an explicit elemental name counts; implicit material presence inside an alloy or functional use as fuel/residue does not count. Under that standard:

* Sn tin. The ordinary Greek name kassiteros / kassiteron is post-Homeric, first Hesiodic/later. Bronze is always chalkos and the constituent tin materially present in every piece of chalkos is never singled out. Canonical Homeric ‘missing metal’, uncontroversial.
* Hg mercury/quicksilver. Hydrargyros / hydrargos is Classical and unattested in Homeric poetry. Native liquid metal known in Near East/Egypt but no Homeric name, uncontroversial.
* Pb lead. Classical name molybdos μόλυβδος is post-Homeric on normal philological dating. No secure Homeric by-name for elemental lead in Odyssey onomasticon. Majority now treats Pb as absent by name on the same strict lexical bar applied to Sn and Hg; remains the most disputed of the three but converging to absent.

Metal-only formulation therefore: Au and Ag named unambiguously, Cu known only as alloyed chalkos, Fe named at best marginally as sideros, Sn, Hg and on strict dating Pb unnamed as distinct elemental substances. Tin is the most conspicuous because it is physically present in every chalkos.

Non-metal extension: Carbon is materially ubiquitous as anthrakes charcoal/soot in hearth/sacrifice/forge scenes e.g. Od.5.59,16.2,18.44,19.389 etc., but treated like implicit tin inside chalkos: functional material, never isolated as an elemental name, and therefore not counted as a nominal omission under the current strict naming criterion. Sulfur theion S is at best allusive in volcanic/brimstone contexts, theion not securely Homeric in Odyssey; arsenic arsenikon As is unattested. Pure Cu as free metal is also never named apart from chalkos.

Unresolved: exact weight to give sideros marginality vs complete absence; whether lead should be treated as definitively absent or merely marginal given molybdos dating disputes; whether the answer should stay metal-only Sn/Hg/Pb or be enlarged to include theion S and/or pure Cu as non-metal/elemental omissions. Current best-supported set under the group’s consistent strict naming criterion is Sn, Hg and Pb, with Sn and Hg uncontroversial and Pb classic on strict reading, and sulfur as the sole defensible non-metal addition if non-metals are admitted. Carbon remains excluded by the same criterion.
reflection_text.6:
The problem is which elements handleable in elemental form c. 8th c BC – Au, Ag, Cu, Fe, Sn, Pb, Hg and the native non-metals S, C, As – Zn and Sb excluded by hypothesis – have no elemental name in the Odyssey.

Current converging lexical inventory:
* Au chrysos and Ag argyros are secure, ubiquitous elemental names.
* chalkos / chalkeos is the poem’s working metal – swords, shields, mixing bowls, tripods, nails etc. In Homeric Greek chalkos is the Cu-Sn alloy we call bronze. Pure copper is never lexically isolated from the alloy; elemental Cu is present only as the composite name chalkos = bronze.
* sideros is attested Od. 1.104, 9.391, 10.235, 15.324, 17.285, 21.10 etc., rare and largely generic ‘hard metal’. Majority treats iron as at least marginally named; Colleague 4 continues to argue earliest secure attestation is Hesiod Works and Days 143 ff. and that in Homer it is effectively absent on a strict Bronze-Age reading. Unresolved.

Canonical absences on strict onomastic dating:
* Sn tin. The ordinary Greek name kassiteros / kassiteron is post-Homeric, first Hesiodic and later. Bronze is always chalkos and the constituent tin materially present in every piece of chalkos is never singled out as a separate substance. The textbook Homeric ‘missing metal’, uncontroversial.
* Hg mercury / quicksilver. Hydrargyros / hydrargos is Classical and unattested in Homeric poetry. The native liquid metal was known in Near East/Egypt but has no Homeric name. Uncontroversial.
* Pb lead. Molybdos is the Classical name and on the normal philological dating used for Homeric diction there is no secure Homeric by-name for elemental lead in the Odyssey onomasticon. On the strict lexical bar applied to Sn and Hg lead is absent by name; a minority allows a looser reading. Round 3 majority keeps Pb in the core trio.

Non-metals / pure copper:
* S sulfur theion: not securely Homeric; volcanic/brimstone allusions are indirect at best. Clearest non-metal omission by name on strict standard; Colleagues 13, 7 now suggest it as the defensible fourth candidate if non-metals are admitted.
* As arsenic arsenikon: unattested.
* C carbon: anthrakes charcoal/soot/smoke is materially ubiquitous Od. 5.59, 16.2, 18.44, 19.389 etc. Group consensus now treats this as functional fuel/residue, never isolated as an elemental label, by the same strict naming criterion that excludes implicit tin inside chalkos. Carbon is therefore not counted as a nominal omission in the metal-focused formulation.
* Pure Cu as a free metal is never named apart from chalkos = bronze.

Strict naming criterion converged on: only an explicit elemental label counts; implicit presence inside an alloy or functional practical use as fuel/residue does not count. This bars implicit tin in chalkos, bars anthrakes as carbon, and bars indirect volcanic allusions to sulfur.

Best-supported metal-only statement: Odyssey names Au and Ag unambiguously, knows Cu only in the alloyed form chalkos/bronze, names Fe at best marginally as sideros, and leaves Sn, Hg and on strict dating Pb unnamed as distinct elemental substances, Sn being the most conspicuous because it is physically present in every piece of chalkos while its name is never given.

Remaining open points: exact lexical status of sideros marginal vs absent; whether Pb stays in core set under strict dating; whether native sulfur theion should be added as a fourth canonical omission on strict naming; whether pure copper deserves separate listing as absent independent name. Zn/Sb remain excluded by hypothesis.
reflection_text.10:
The pre-classical inventory under discussion is Au, Ag, Cu, Fe, Sn, Pb, Hg, plus the native non-metals S theion, C as anthrakes charcoal/soot, As arsenikon. Zn and Sb are excluded by hypothesis.

Attested Homeric nomenclature in the Odyssey:
* chrysos = Au gold, ubiquitous.
* argyros = Ag silver, ubiquitous.
* chalkos / chalkeos = the poem’s working metal, the Cu–Sn alloy we call bronze. It is named for arms, bowls, tripods etc. Pure copper is never lexically separated from the alloy; elemental Cu has no independent name.
* sideros = Fe iron is contested. Citations repeatedly given are Od. 1.104, 9.391, 15.324, 17.285, 21.10 etc. Majority in round 3 read these as rare/generic ‘hard metal’ uses and count Fe as at best marginal; a minority treats it as absent/securely post-Hesiodic. The Bronze-Age diction remains the dominant framing.

Unattested / post-Homeric names on the strict lexical standard now converged on:
* Sn tin = kassiteros/kassiteron. Consensus: no Homeric attestation. Bronze is always chalkos; tin as a distinct elemental substance is never named. Canonical Homeric missing metal, materially present in every piece of chalkos.
* Hg mercury/quicksilver = hydrargyros/hydrargos. Consensus: unattested in the Homeric corpus.
* Pb lead = molybdos/molubdos. Strict philological dating treats molybdos as post-Homeric; on that bar lead is absent by name in the same way as tin and mercury. A minority allows Homeric attestations, but round 3 converges on absence on the strict reading.
Native non-metals:
* S sulfur = theion. No secure elemental name in Odyssey; at most indirect volcanic/brimstone allusions. Colleagues 10-12,13 treat S as the clearest non-metal omission by name.
* As arsenic = arsenikon. In same position as S, unattested.
* C carbon. Charcoal/anthrakes/soot is materially ubiquitous, e.g. Od. 5.59, 16.2, 18.44, 19.389. Colleagues 1,10,12,14,2,3,4,6,8,9 now argue anthrakes functions like implicit tin inside chalkos: functional material encountered in daily use, never isolated by a lexical label that counts as elemental recognition. Carbon therefore is not counted as a nominal omission under the strict naming criterion. Disagreement persists with earlier rounds that wanted C included.

Disagreements retained:
* Whether sideros is a secure Homeric elemental name or a rare/generic late intrusion, i.e. whether Fe should be counted as mentioned.
* Whether chalkos counts as a mention of pure elemental Cu or only of the alloy.
* Whether sulfur and/or carbon count as “mentioned”. Sulfur is generally taken as absent by name; carbon is materially implied via charcoal but never named elementally, and the group has converged on not counting it.

Current best synthesis after round 3: On the seven classical metals Au Ag Cu Fe Sn Pb Hg, the Odyssey unambiguously names Au and Ag, knows Cu only in the alloy form chalkos = bronze, names Fe at best marginally as sideros. The three classical metals known in elemental form c.800 BCE but without an elemental name in the Odyssey are the canonical Sn tin, Hg mercury/quicksilver, and on strict dating Pb lead. Tin is the textbook conspicuous omission because it is materially present in every piece of chalkos.

If non-metals are admitted, native sulphur theion is likewise without a secure Homeric name; arsenic is in the same position. Pure copper as a free metal and, on strictest reading, iron and sulfur remain unnamed as elements. The metal-only conventionally quoted answer remains Sn, Pb, Hg, with Sn and Hg uncontroversial, Pb third on strict philology.

Unresolved: exact status of sideros/Fe and molybdos/Pb under the strict vs. permissive dating, and whether the question setter wants non-metals S/C/As added to the omission list.
reflection_text.12:
The discussion remains anchored on c.8th c. BCE Homeric metal/non-metal lexicon and the explicit exclusion of Zn and Sb.

Common ground that persists across rounds:
* chrysos = Au gold and argyros = Ag silver are ubiquitous and unambiguously elemental.
* chalkos χαλκός / chalkeos is the poem’s working metal. In Homeric diction chalkos is the Cu-Sn alloy bronze; pure copper is never lexically isolated from the alloy, so an independent elemental name for elemental Cu is absent, Cu is present only as chalkos = bronze.
* The pre-classical inventory in play is Au Ag Cu Fe Sn Pb Hg plus native non-metals S theion, As arsenikon and C as anthrakes charcoal/soot.

Current-round convergence:
* Sn tin kassiteros κασσίτερος is unanimously absent by name. Bronze is always chalkos and the tin component is never singled out; kassiteros is post-Homeric. Tin is the textbook conspicuous omission because it is materially present in every piece of chalkos.
* Hg mercury/quicksilver hydrargyros ὑδράργυρος is unanimously absent by name in Odyssey/Iliad. The liquid metal was known in Near East/Egypt but has no Homeric name.
* Pb lead molybdos μόλυβδος is now the dominant strict reading: colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,6,8,4 treat molybdos as post-Homeric and lead as unattested as a free metal in the Odyssey. The earlier loose claim of Homeric lead is now marginal in current round.

Iron sideros σίδηρος remains contested but majority editorial reading is accepted.
* Many colleagues cite Od.1.104, 9.391, 15.324, 17.285, 21.10 etc. and accept a rare/generic ‘hard metal’ usage, i.e. iron is at least marginally named.
* Colleagues 4,12,8 argue earliest secure sideros is Hesiod WD 143 ff. and that on a strict Bronze-Age lexical reading iron is essentially absent as an ordinary working metal. The strictest reading would therefore also omit Fe.

Non-metals:
* S sulfur theion θείον is widely argued absent as an elemental name; volcanic/brimstone allusions are indirect. Colleagues 10,11,12,3,6,7 flag it as a strict omission. Colleague 13 repeatedly proposes sulfur as a defensible fourth non-metal omission rather than carbon.
* C carbon is materially present as anthrakes/soot in cooking, sacrifice and forge scenes, Od.5.59,16.2,18.44 etc. Colleagues 1,13 originally included it, but current round 13,14,5,9,7 treat inclusion as weak: the poem uses practical material, not an elemental name, and same standard that bars implicit tin within chalkos bars implicit carbon. Consensus now rejects carbon as a nominal omission.
* As arsenic realgar/orpiment is without a secure Homeric name.

Unresolved/live questions:
* Exact status of sideros as attested elemental name vs generic hard metal; whether to count Fe as named or absent on strictest Bronze-Age reading.
* Whether molybdos lead is to be counted as truly absent by name or allowed a loose reading; current weight is strict absence.
* Whether pure copper should be listed as unnamed because it only appears as chalkos/bronze; group treats this as lexical absence but textbook formulation focuses on Sn/Pb/Hg.
* Whether sulfur theion counts as ‘mentioned’ via indirect volcanic/brimstone references; current trend is it does not meet naming criterion, and Colleague 7 notes it as the only plausible non-metal addition without relaxing the lexical standard.

Overall trend:
Au and Ag are securely named; Cu is present only as alloy chalkos; Fe is marginal. The textbook Homeric omissions by name are Sn tin and Hg mercury, with Pb lead as the third classic absent metal on strict philology, and S sulfur as the clearest non-metal omission on a strict lexical reading. Tin-lead-mercury is the conventionally quoted set, tin being most conspicuous because it is materially present in every piece of chalkos. Carbon is not counted as an omission under the strict naming standard now converged on.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The lexical standard that has now been applied uniformly across the discussion—only an explicit, distinct elemental name counts as recognition—continues to single out the three post-Homeric metals as the clearest omissions. Kassiteros, molybdos and hydrargyros are all unattested in the Odyssey, while the substances themselves were already being handled in relatively pure native form by the eighth century.  

References to anthrakes or soot remain functional descriptions of fuel and residue, exactly parallel to the way tin is materially present inside every occurrence of chalkos yet never isolated by name; the same criterion that correctly withholds elemental status from the alloy component also withholds it from carbon. Volcanic or brimstone passages for theion are still more oblique and likewise fail to supply a secure elemental label.  

Colleague 13’s suggestion to enlarge the set with sulfur therefore introduces the same relaxation of the naming test that the group has already rejected for carbon. Retaining the compact, philologically consistent set—tin, lead and mercury—preserves the strict Bronze-Age onomastic filter that the poem itself exhibits and aligns with the historical record of substances worked in elemental form at the time of composition.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The emerging consensus remains the most coherent and philologically disciplined reading of the Odyssey’s restricted Bronze-Age lexicon. Only chrysos, argyros, the alloy chalkos, and the marginal/generic sideros receive any elemental or near-elemental naming; the post-Homeric status of kassiteros, molybdos and hydrargyros therefore keeps tin, lead and mercury as the three metals already handled in relatively pure native form by the eighth century yet never isolated by a distinct Homeric term.  

The same strict onomastic filter that bars any independent lexical recognition of the tin constituent latent in every occurrence of chalkos also bars carbon: repeated references to anthrakes or soot are functional descriptions of fuel or residue in hearths and forges (Od. 5.59, 16.2, 18.44, 19.389), never an explicit elemental label comparable to chrysos for gold. Adding sulfur on the basis of indirect volcanic or brimstone allusions would require precisely the relaxation of the naming criterion that the group has already rejected for carbon and for implicit copper apart from the alloy. Retaining the compact three-metal set—tin, lead and mercury—therefore aligns most cleanly with both the poem’s diction and the historical inventory of substances worked in elemental form at the time of composition, without introducing inconsistent enlargements of the omission set.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The lexical standard that has guided the discussion continues to supply the clearest filter: only substances isolated by an explicit elemental name in the Odyssey’s Bronze-Age diction qualify. Chrysos and argyros name gold and silver without ambiguity; chalkos consistently denotes the Cu–Sn alloy without ever separating its tin constituent; sideros appears only marginally. Kassiteros, molybdos and hydrargyros remain unattested, so the three metals already handled in native form by the eighth century—tin, lead and mercury—stand as the canonical omissions.  

Colleague 13’s suggestion of sulfur (theion) as a possible fourth element is worth testing against the same criterion. Volcanic or brimstone passages supply only indirect allusion, never the secure elemental label itself, so sulfur fails the naming test in precisely the same way that practical references to anthrakes fail it for carbon. Adding sulfur would therefore require relaxing the lexical standard the group has applied uniformly to the metals, while the compact three-metal set (tin, lead, mercury) preserves that standard intact and matches both the poem’s restricted onomasticon and the historical record of substances worked in elemental form at the time of composition.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The emerging group consensus on tin, lead and mercury as the canonical omissions remains the most coherent and philologically consistent reading. The Odyssey’s substance vocabulary is a Bronze-Age vocabulary.

* chrysos χρυσός = Au and argyros ἀργυρός = Ag are elemental and ubiquitous.
* chalkos χαλκός / chalkeos is the normal working metal of the poem – swords, shields, mixing bowls, tripods, nails etc. In Homeric Greek chalkos is the Cu-Sn alloy we call bronze. Pure copper is never lexically isolated from the alloy; elemental Cu is present only as the composite name chalkos = bronze.
* sideros σίδηρος is attested Od. 1.104, 9.391, 15.324, 17.285, 21.10 etc. On the usual editorial reading iron is named, albeit rare and essentially generic ‘hard metal’. On the strictest Bronze-Age reading it is marginal.

Zn and Sb are put out of court by the question. Of the pre-classical inventory that could be handled in the Eastern Mediterranean c.800 BC

Au Ag Cu Fe Sn Pb Hg

Au and Ag are named unambiguously, Fe is named at best marginally as sideros and Cu is known only in the alloyed form chalkos = bronze.

The three classical metals which were already being handled in relatively pure native form in the Late Bronze / early Iron Age East Mediterranean but which have no elemental name in the Homeric onomasticon are the textbook omissions.

* Sn tin. The ordinary Greek name kassiteros / kassiteron is post-Homeric, first securely Hesiodic and later. Bronze is always named as chalkos and the constituent tin that is materially present in every piece of chalkos that Homer describes is never singled out as a separate substance. That is the canonical Homeric silence on tin.
* Hg mercury / quicksilver. Hydrargyros ὑδράργυρος / hydrargos is Classical and unattested in Homeric poetry. The native liquid metal was known in the Near East/Egypt but it has no Homeric name in either Iliad or Odyssey.
* Pb lead. The Classical name molybdos μόλυβδος is post-Homeric on the normal philological dating used for Homeric diction. Lead is therefore absent by name from the Odyssey onomasticon on the same strict lexical bar that removes tin and mercury. Tin and mercury are uncontroversial; lead is the third classic absent metal on strict dating.

On the same strict naming criterion pure copper is never named apart from the alloy chalkos = bronze and the native non-metals that were in ordinary Bronze Age use are likewise without a secure Homeric elemental name. The clearest non-metal example is S sulphur theion, volcanic/brimstone allusions being indirect and theion not securely Homeric in the Odyssey. Carbon is materially ubiquitous as anthrakes charcoal/soot in hearth, sacrifice, cooking and forge scenes, Od.5.59,16.2,18.44,19.389 etc., and under the strict naming standard now converged on it is not counted as a nominal omission in the metal-focused formulation.

In the normal metal-only statement the Odyssey names Au and Ag, knows Cu only as the alloy chalkos/bronze, names Fe at least marginally as sideros, and leaves Sn, Pb and Hg unnamed as distinct elemental substances, Sn being the most conspicuous because it is physically present in every piece of chalkos the poem describes. If the inventory is extended to native non-metals theion S is the clearest further omission by name, while anthrakes is functional material, not elemental naming.

The Odyssey’s substance vocabulary is a Bronze-Age vocabulary.

* chrysos χρυσός = Au and argyros ἀργυρός = Ag are elemental and ubiquitous.
* chalkos χαλκός / chalkeos is the normal working metal of the poem – swords, shields, mixing bowls, tripods, nails etc. In Homeric Greek chalkos is the Cu-Sn alloy we call bronze. Pure copper is never lexically isolated from the alloy; elemental Cu is present only as the composite name chalkos = bronze.
* sideros σίδηρος is attested Od. 1.104, 9.391, 15.324, 17.285, 21.10 etc. On the usual editorial reading iron is named, albeit rare and essentially generic ‘hard metal’. On the strictest Bronze-Age reading it is marginal.

Zn and Sb are put out of court by the question. Of the pre-classical inventory that could be handled in the Eastern Mediterranean c.800 BC

Au Ag Cu Fe Sn Pb Hg

Au and Ag are named unambiguously, Fe is named at best marginally as sideros and Cu is known only in the alloyed form chalkos = bronze.

The three classical metals which were already being handled in relatively pure native form in the Late Bronze / early Iron Age East Mediterranean but which have no elemental name in the Homeric onomasticon are the textbook omissions.

* Sn tin. The ordinary Greek name kassiteros / kassiteron is post-Homeric, first securely Hesiodic and later. Bronze is always named as chalkos and the constituent tin that is materially present in every piece of chalkos that Homer describes is never singled out as a separate substance. That is the canonical Homeric silence on tin.
* Hg mercury / quicksilver. Hydrargyros ὑδράργυρος / hydrargos is Classical and unattested in Homeric poetry. The native liquid metal was known in the Near East/Egypt but it has no Homeric name in either Iliad or Odyssey.
* Pb lead. The Classical name molybdos μόλυβδος is post-Homeric on the normal philological dating used for Homeric diction. Lead is therefore absent by name from the Odyssey onomasticon on the same strict lexical bar that removes tin and mercury. Tin and mercury are uncontroversial; lead is the third classic absent metal on strict dating.

On the same strict naming criterion pure copper is never named apart from the alloy chalkos = bronze and the native non-metals that were in ordinary Bronze Age use are likewise without a secure Homeric elemental name. The clearest non-metal example is S sulphur theion, volcanic/brimstone allusions being indirect and theion not securely Homeric in the Odyssey. Carbon is materially ubiquitous as anthrakes charcoal/soot in hearth, sacrifice, cooking and forge scenes, Od.5.59,16.2,18.44,19.389 etc., and under the strict naming standard now converged on it is not counted as a nominal omission in the metal-focused formulation.

In the normal metal-only statement the Odyssey names Au and Ag, knows Cu only as the alloy chalkos/bronze, names Fe at least marginally as sideros, and leaves Sn, Pb and Hg unnamed as distinct elemental substances, Sn being the most conspicuous because it is physically present in every piece of chalkos the poem describes. If the inventory is extended to native non-metals theion S is the clearest further omission by name, while anthrakes is functional material, not elemental naming.

reflection_text.3:
The deliberation has converged on a strict onomastic criterion: only an independent elemental name in the Odyssey counts; material presence inside an alloy or functional fuel/residue does not.

Securely named:
* Au chrysos gold – ubiquitous.
* Ag argyros silver – ubiquitous.
* chalkos / chalkeos – the poem’s working metal, swords, shields, bowls, tripods etc. In Homeric Greek chalkos is the Cu–Sn alloy we call bronze. Pure copper is never lexically isolated from the alloy; elemental Cu is present only as the composite name chalkos = bronze.
* sideros – Fe iron is attested Od. 1.104, 9.391, 15.324, 17.285, 21.10 etc. Use is rare and largely generic ‘hard metal’. Colleagues 10,2,3,6,8 treat attestations as real albeit marginal. Colleague 4,12 keep the strict Bronze-Age reading that sideros is marginal/generic and iron is effectively absent as an ordinary working element. Weight stays with marginal attestation.

Demonstrably absent by name on the strict post-Homeric dating:
* Sn tin – kassiteros/kassiteron is post-Homeric, first Hesiodic/later. Bronze is always chalkos and the constituent Sn is never singled out. Materially present in every piece of chalkos described. Uncontested canonical absence.
* Hg mercury / quicksilver – hydrargyros/hydrargos is unattested in Homeric poetry. Native liquid metal known Near East/Egypt but no Homeric name. Uncontested canonical absence.
* Pb lead – molybdos is the Classical name, post-Homeric on normal philological dating. No secure Homeric by-name for elemental lead in Odyssey onomasticon. Colleagues 10,2,3,6,8,11,12,4 treat Pb as absent by name on the same strict test applied to Sn/Hg; the metal-only set is therefore Sn, Hg and on strict dating Pb. Tin and mercury are the uncontroversial core, lead the third classic absent metal.

Non-metals under the same naming test:
* S sulfur – theion is not securely Homeric. Volcanic/brimstone allusions remain indirect. Most colleagues now treat sulfur as absent by name on a strict lexical standard. Colleagues 10,11,12,3,7,13 note it as the clearest non-metal omission if non-metals are counted.
* C carbon – anthrakes charcoal/soot appear repeatedly in cooking, sacrifice, forge, hearth, e.g. Od. 5.59, 16.2, 18.44, 19.389. Colleagues 5,9,13 argued material presence should count. Round 2-3 consensus converges that these are functional fuel/residue references, exactly parallel to implicit tin inside chalkos; same strict naming standard bars implicit carbon. Carbon is now generally not counted as a nominal omission. Colleague 14,5,9 explicitly reject carbon enlargement.
* As arsenic – realgar/orpiment also without secure Homeric elemental name, noted by 11,12.

Zinc and antimony are excluded by hypothesis.

Current synthesis: On the seven classical metals Au Ag Cu Fe Sn Pb Hg, Au and Ag are uncontested elemental mentions, Cu is present only as the alloy chalkos/bronze, Fe is marginally attested as sideros. The robust, uncontested elemental omissions by name are Sn tin and Hg mercury, with Pb lead as the third classic absent metal on strict post-Homeric dating of molybdos. Sn is the textbook canonical omission because it is materially present in every chalkos object. Sulfur theion is the clearest non-metal omission by name on a strict reading. Carbon is materially ubiquitous via charcoal/soot and is now generally not counted as omitted. Iron remains residual dispute between rare attested sideros and effective absence on strict Bronze-Age lexical reading. Pure copper as an isolated element is also unnamed.

Unresolved tension: whether to list Pb as fully absent or marginal – majority now treats it as absent on strict dating – and whether to extend the inventory to non-metals S. The metal-only formulation most colleagues share is Sn, Pb, Hg absent, with Sn and Hg uncontroversial. If non-metals are admitted, S theion is the defensible fourth candidate; carbon is no longer argued for under the consistent naming test.

reflection_text.2:

On strictest elemental naming pure Cu and S also lack Homeric elemental name, and Fe remains marginal. The cleanest answer for the metal-focused question is Sn, Hg and on strict dating Pb; if non-metals are admitted, theion S is the most defensible fourth nominal omission.
reflection_text.4:
The deliberation remains anchored on Homeric elemental vocabulary c.800 BCE with Zn and Sb excluded by the prompt.

Common ground now stable across rounds 0-4:
* chrysos = Au gold and argyros = Ag silver are ubiquitous and uncontroversial elemental names.
* chalkos χαλκός is the working metal of the poem, used constantly for weapons, bowls, tripods etc. It is bronze Cu–Sn. Homer never disentangles pure copper from the alloy; pure Cu is therefore never named as a distinct elemental substance, only as the alloy.

Current best synthesis from rounds 0-4:
Elements known in elemental form c.800 BCE that are named in the Odyssey are gold and silver unequivocally, iron on the looser reading, and copper only in alloyed form chalkos = bronze. On a strict lexical reading iron is also effectively absent.
