Current-round convergence:
* Sn tin kassiteros κασσίτερος is unanimously absent by name. Bronze is always chalkos and the tin component is never singled out; kassiteros is post-Homeric. Tin is the textbook conspicuous omission because it is materially present in every piece of chalkos.
* Hg mercury/quicksilver hydrargyros ὑδράργυρος is unanimously absent by name in Odyssey/Iliad. Liquid metal known in Near East/Egypt but has no Homeric name.
* Pb lead molybdos μόλυβδος is now dominant strict reading: colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,6,8,4 treat molybdos as post-Homeric and lead as unattested as a free metal in the Odyssey. Earlier loose claim of Homeric lead is now marginal.

Iron sideros σίδηρος remains contested but majority editorial reading is accepted as marginal/generic hard metal.
* Many cite Od.1.104, 9.391, 15.324, 17.285, 21.10 etc. and accept rare/generic usage → iron at least marginally named.
* Colleagues 4,12,8 argue earliest secure sideros is Hesiod WD 143 ff. and that on strict Bronze-Age lexical reading iron is essentially absent as an ordinary working metal. Strictest reading would also omit Fe.

Non-metals:
* S sulfur theion θείον is widely argued absent as an elemental name; volcanic/brimstone allusions are indirect. Colleagues 10,11,12,3,6,7 flag it as a strict omission. Colleague 13 repeatedly proposes sulfur as defensible fourth non-metal omission rather than carbon.
* C carbon is materially present as anthrakes/soot in cooking, sacrifice, forge scenes Od.5.59,16.2,18.44 etc. Colleagues 1,13 originally included it, but current round 13,14,5,9,7 treat inclusion as weak: poem uses practical material, not elemental name, and same standard that bars implicit tin within chalkos bars implicit carbon. Consensus now rejects carbon as a nominal omission.
* As arsenic realgar/orpiment is without secure Homeric name.

Unresolved/live questions:
* Exact status of sideros as attested elemental name vs generic hard metal; whether to count Fe as named or absent on strictest Bronze-Age reading.
* Whether molybdos lead is to be counted as truly absent by name or allowed a loose reading; current weight is strict absence.
* Whether pure copper should be listed as unnamed because it only appears as chalkos/bronze; group treats this as lexical absence but textbook formulation focuses on Sn/Pb/Hg.
* Whether sulfur theion counts as ‘mentioned’ via indirect volcanic/brimstone references; current trend is it does not meet naming criterion, and Colleague 7 notes it as only plausible non-metal addition without relaxing lexical standard.

Overall trend:
Au and Ag securely named; Cu present only as alloy chalkos; Fe marginal. Textbook Homeric omissions by name are Sn tin and Hg mercury, with Pb lead as third classic absent metal on strict philology, and S sulfur as clearest non-metal omission on strict lexical reading. Tin-lead-mercury is conventionally quoted set, tin most conspicuous because materially present in every piece of chalkos. Carbon is not counted as an omission under strict naming standard now converged on.
reflection_text.6:
The inventory that can be handled in elemental form c.800 BC, with Zn and Sb excluded by hypothesis, is Au, Ag, Cu, Fe, Sn, Pb, Hg and the native non-metals S, As and C as anthrakes charcoal/soot. The group has converged on a strict onomastic criterion: only an explicit elemental name in the Odyssey counts as a mention; material presence inside an alloy or functional use as fuel/residue does not.

Secure names:
* chrysos = Au and argyros = Ag are elemental and ubiquitous.
* chalkos / chalkeos is the poem’s working metal. In Homeric Greek chalkos is the Cu–Sn alloy we call bronze. Pure copper is never lexically isolated from the alloy; elemental Cu is present only as the composite name chalkos = bronze.
* sideros is attested Od. 1.104, 9.391, 10.235, 15.324, 17.285, 21.10 etc., rare and essentially generic ‘hard metal’. Editorial majority treats iron as at least marginally named; Colleague 4 continues the strict Bronze-Age view that secure attestation is Hesiodic and Homeric use is marginal. This remains unresolved.

Canonical metal absences on strict dating:
* Sn tin. The ordinary Greek name kassiteros / kassiteron is post-Homeric, first securely Hesiodic and later. Bronze is always chalkos and the constituent tin materially present in every piece of chalkos is never singled out as a separate substance. The textbook Homeric ‘missing metal’, uncontroversial.
* Hg mercury / quicksilver. Hydrargyros / hydrargos is Classical and unattested in Homeric poetry. The native liquid metal was known in the Near East/Egypt but has no Homeric name. Uncontroversial.
* Pb lead. Molybdos is the Classical name. On the strict lexicographical dating normally used for Homeric diction there is no secure Homeric by-name for elemental lead in the Odyssey onomasticon. On the strict reading used for Sn and Hg lead is therefore absent by name; a minority allows a looser reading. Round 4 majority keeps Pb in the core trio, with Sn and Hg the uncontroversial canonical pair.

Non-metals / pure copper under the same strict test:
* Pure Cu as a free metal is never named apart from chalkos = bronze.
* S sulfur theion: not securely Homeric; volcanic/brimstone allusions are indirect at best. The clearest non-metal omission by name on strict standard. Colleague 13 now argues for it as the defensible fourth candidate if non-metals are admitted; Colleagues 1,14,7,5 argue it fails the same naming test as carbon and should not be added without relaxing the criterion.
* As arsenic arsenikon: unattested.
* C carbon: anthrakes charcoal/soot/smoke is materially ubiquitous Od.5.59,16.2,18.44,19.389 etc. Group consensus treats this as functional fuel/residue, never isolated as an elemental label, by the same strict naming criterion that excludes implicit tin inside chalkos. Carbon is therefore not counted as a nominal omission in the metal-focused formulation, and would require the same relaxation that would be needed for sulfur.

Current belief: the clean, philologically coherent metal-only statement is Odyssey names Au and Ag unambiguously, knows Cu only in the alloyed form chalkos/bronze, names Fe at best marginally as sideros, and leaves Sn, Hg and on strict philology Pb unnamed as distinct elemental substances, Sn being the most conspicuous because it is physically present in every piece of chalkos while its name is never given. If non-metals are admitted to the inventory, theion S is the most defensible additional nominal omission on the strict lexical criterion, while anthrakes is functional material not elemental naming. Unresolved open points remain the exact lexical status of sideros marginal vs absent, whether Pb stays in the core set under strict dating, and whether sulfur should be added as a fourth canonical omission. Zn/Sb remain excluded by hypothesis.
